nameStory: The scientific name "interpres" comes from the Latin word for "interpreter" or "go-between," though the exact reason this tiny spider earned this diplomatic title remains a mystery. Like many dwarf spiders, it may have gotten this name from early taxonomists who saw these minuscule creatures as intermediaries between the spider world we can easily see and the hidden realm of the truly microscopic.
description: Ceratinopsis interpres is a dwarf spider so tiny you might mistake it for a speck of dust at first glance. These minuscule arachnids belong to the sheetweb weaver family, known for creating delicate, flat webs that look like tiny trampolines stretched between vegetation. While we don't have exact size measurements, like other dwarf spiders, this species is likely only a few millimeters long with a compact, rounded body typical of its family.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small - often just a few millimeters long, requiring close inspection or magnification to see details clearly

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates tiny sheet webs that feel delicate and papery when accidentally brushed, stretched horizontally between low vegetation

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and rounded with a relatively large abdomen compared to other body parts, giving it a somewhat balloon-like appearance

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions when disturbed and tends to drop from its web rather than run across it

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight tiny eyes arranged in two rows, though you'll need magnification to see this arrangement clearly

habitat: Look for this rare spider in low vegetation areas like meadow edges, forest clearings, and grassy areas where it can string its tiny sheet webs between plant stems. Given its extremely limited observation records in New England, it likely prefers specific microhabitats that we're still learning about. You'll need to search carefully in areas with dense, low-growing plants where its miniature webs can be anchored close to the ground.

seasonality.spring: Adults may become active as temperatures warm, beginning to build their tiny sheet webs in emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be spotted on their webs and potentially mating.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, with egg-laying likely occurring before winter arrives.
seasonality.winter: Probably overwinters as eggs or juveniles hidden in leaf litter and soil, with adults not visible.

funFact: This spider is so rare in New England that it's only been reliably documented twice in the entire region - making every sighting a genuine scientific treasure that could help us understand its mysterious distribution patterns!
confusionNotes: With only two confirmed observations in New England, this spider is more likely to be overlooked entirely than confused with other species. Any tiny spider in a small sheet web could potentially be this species, but definitive identification requires expert examination due to the many similar dwarf spider species in our region.
contextualKnowledge: The family name Linyphiidae comes from the Greek word for "flax" or "linen," referring to the fine, sheet-like webs these spiders create that early naturalists thought resembled delicate fabric. Despite being called "dwarf" spiders, this family is actually one of the largest spider families in the world.
compareHints: Since this is the only Ceratinopsis species documented in our dataset for New England, compare it with other dwarf spiders in the Linyphiidae family by focusing on its extremely small size and horizontal sheet webs. Unlike some other linyphiids that build more complex webs with knockdown threads, Ceratinopsis interpres likely creates simpler, flatter sheet structures. The rarity of sightings also distinguishes it from more common dwarf spiders you might encounter.
